name: Ancien Régime France
title: Social Hierarchy of Ancien Régime France: From King to Enslaved
period: 1715–1789 (from the death of Louis XIV to the Revolution)

tiers.name: The king
tiers.you: You were anointed at Reims and can imprison a subject without trial, but the parlements can delay your edicts and debts weigh on your treasury.
tiers.kid: The king lived in the great palace of Versailles and was crowned in the cathedral of Reims.
tiers.rise: The crown passed from father to son in the male line, and Louis XV, whose son had died, left it to his grandson Louis XVI in 1774. A king who came to the throne as a child, as Louis XV did, ruled through a regent until he came of age.
tiers.why: The king stood outside and above the three orders.

tiers.name: Bishops and abbots
tiers.you: As a younger son of a noble family you were destined for the church; you govern a diocese, may sit on the king’s councils and may live at court rather than in your diocese.
tiers.kid: Bishops were powerful churchmen from noble families, and the church they led owned rich lands.
tiers.rise: Bishoprics and rich abbeys went to the younger sons of noble families, chosen by the king and his ministers. By the 1780s a commoner could no longer hope for a bishopric.
tiers.why: The clergy formed the First Estate, the senior order, and its leaders lived as great lords.

tiers.name: Nobles
tiers.term: noblesse, noblesse d'épée, noblesse de robe
tiers.you: You pay no taille, wear a sword and may hunt, and if your family has been noble for four generations you may be commissioned an officer, but trade or manual work would cost you your nobility.
tiers.kid: Nobles did not have to pay the taille, the main tax that ordinary French families paid.
tiers.rise: Nobility came by birth, by royal letters, or by buying an office that ennobled its holder: that of secrétaire du roi cost 120,000 livres in 1773 and was mocked as a savonnette à vilain, a soap that washed away common birth. On one estimate, some 6,000 families had been ennobled through office by 1765.
tiers.why: The nobles formed the Second Estate: perhaps 120,000 to 400,000 people, as estimates differ widely, holding some 25 to 30 per cent of the land.

tiers.name: Parish priests, monks and nuns
tiers.term: bas clergé, curés, vicaires, religieux, religieuses
tiers.you: You serve a parish on a fixed stipend while its tithe goes to a bishop or an abbey; you baptise, marry and bury your parishioners and have more in common with them than with your bishop.
tiers.kid: Village priests ran the parish church, and many of them earned very little money.
tiers.rise: The priesthood was open to commoners who could be trained for it, but few rose higher, since bishoprics went to nobles; a priest’s rank was his own and passed to no heirs.
tiers.why: Below the prelates stood the great body of the clergy: the curés and their curates (vicaires) of some 40,000 parish churches, and the monks and nuns of the religious houses.

tiers.name: The bourgeoisie
tiers.you: You live from trade, the law or an office and put your profits into land; you pay the taille unless your town or your office spares you, and noble privilege still bars your way.
tiers.kid: The bourgeois were well-off townspeople, such as merchants, bankers and lawyers.
tiers.rise: Merchants’ sons became lawyers and officeholders, and the richest families bought ennobling offices or married into poor noble families. From 1781 the army’s officer commissions were closed to them.
tiers.why: At the top of the Third Estate stood the bourgeoisie: merchants and bankers, financiers and tax farmers, lawyers, notaries and doctors, the holders of venal offices, and rentiers living on their investments.

tiers.name: Artisans and workers of the towns
tiers.you: You work in a master’s shop or keep your own, under your guild’s rules, and in a bad year bread can swallow half or more of your family’s income.
tiers.kid: Craftspeople in towns belonged to guilds, groups that set the rules for each trade, such as baking.
tiers.rise: A journeyman became a master by passing the guild’s tests and paying its fees. In 1776 the minister Turgot abolished the guilds’ privileges, but they were soon restored after his fall that same year.
tiers.why: About a fifth of the French lived in towns, and Paris alone had 600,000 to 650,000 people.

tiers.name: Peasants
tiers.you: You farm a small plot of your own or someone else’s land, pay the taille, the tithe and your lord’s dues, must use his mill, and fear every bad harvest.
tiers.kid: Most French people were peasants, who farmed the land and paid taxes to the king, the church and their lord.
tiers.rise: A family rose by buying land and leasing more, and the sons of prosperous farmers became priests, notaries or merchants. Debt, bad harvests and divided inheritances pushed others down into day labour, and many left for the towns.
tiers.why: Peasants were the great majority, at least four people in five, and they ranged from rich farmers to the landless.

tiers.name: Serfs
tiers.you: You farm your own holding like your neighbours, but as a mainmortable you know that your land and goods will go to your lord unless your heirs live under your roof.
tiers.kid: A few French farmers were still serfs in 1789 and had fewer rights than their neighbours.
tiers.rise: Lords could free their serfs, and the crown freed its own in 1779. The rest were freed in August 1789.
tiers.why: Serfdom had faded from most of France long before the 18th century, but it survived in pockets of the east and centre, above all on the lands of churches and abbeys in Franche-Comté, Burgundy, Berry and the Marche.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You were shipped from Africa to a plantation in the French West Indies and are property: you can be sold and your children will be born enslaved, but if your owner takes you to France you may sue for your freedom.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people were owned by others and made to work without pay on plantations in France’s colonies.
tiers.rise: Freedom came by manumission, by purchase or, in France, by a lawsuit, and the Code Noir gave freed slaves the rights of free subjects.
tiers.why: Slavery had no place in the law of France itself: the soil of France was held to make free, and enslaved people brought from the colonies fled or sued for their freedom, and some French courts declared them free.
